title: Valid Palindrome
summary: After lower-casing letters and dropping every character that is not a letter or digit, does the string read the same both ways?

in: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

statement:
A phrase counts as a palindrome if, once you turn every uppercase letter into lowercase and throw away everything that is not a letter or a digit, it reads the same forwards and backwards.

Given a string `s`, return `true` if it is a palindrome under that rule and `false` otherwise. A string that has no letters or digits at all (for example `" "` or `".,"`) is empty after cleaning, and an empty string is a palindrome.
constraints: s contains printable ASCII characters only
hints: You never need to build the cleaned string. Can you compare characters of the original string directly?
Put one pointer at each end. Skip any character that is not a letter or digit, then compare the two characters you are left on.
Compare with Character.toLowerCase on both sides, and stop as soon as the pointers meet or cross. That is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
explain: Keeping only letters and digits and lower-casing them gives "amanaplanacanalpanama", which reads the same backwards. So the answer is `true`.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
summary: Given a sorted array, keep one copy of each value at the front, in order, in place, and return how many unique values there are. The judge prints k and the first k elements.
call: int[] a = BCB.IA($0); int k = s.removeDuplicates(a); Object r = new Object[] { k, Arrays.copyOf(a, Math.max(0, Math.min(k, a.length))) };

perf.label: n = 30,000
perf.call: int k = s.removeDuplicates(a0); Object r = new Object[] { k, Arrays.copyOf(a0, Math.max(0, Math.min(k, a0.length))) };

statement:
`nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order. Rearrange it in place so that each distinct value appears exactly once at the front of the array, in the same order as before, and return `k`, the number of distinct values.

Only the first `k` positions matter; whatever is left after them is ignored. Do it without allocating another array. The judge prints `k` followed by the first `k` elements.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Because the array is sorted, all copies of a value sit next to each other. How do you know a value is new?
Keep a write pointer w for the next free slot of the answer. Scan with a read pointer; copy a value to nums[w] only when it differs from the last value you wrote.
Compare against nums[w - 1] (the last value kept), not nums[i - 1]. Return w at the end.
explain: The distinct values are 1 and 2, so k is 2 and the first two slots of `nums` must hold 1, 2. The tests show this as `[2,[1,2]]`: k, then the first k elements.

title: Move Zeroes
summary: Move every 0 to the end of the array in place, keeping the other values in their original order. The judge prints the array after your call.
statement:
Move every `0` in `nums` to the end of the array while keeping all non-zero values in their original relative order. Change the array in place; do not make a copy.

The method returns nothing. The judge prints `nums` after your call.
hints: Think of it as "keep the non-zero values, in order, at the front".
Use a write pointer: copy each non-zero value to nums[w++] as you scan.
After the scan, every position from w to the end should be 0. Fill them in, or swap instead of copying so the zeros move back on their own.
explain: The non-zero values 1, 3 and 12 keep their order and move to the front, and the two zeros go to the end: `[1,3,12,0,0]`.

title: Squares of a Sorted Array
summary: Given a sorted array that may contain negatives, return the squares of its values in sorted order — ideally in O(n).
statement:
`nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order and may contain negative numbers. Return a new array with the square of every value, also sorted in non-decreasing order.

Squaring then sorting works in O(n log n). The interesting solution runs in O(n).
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Where in the input are the largest squares? Think about large negative values.
The biggest square is always at one of the two ends. Compare the absolute values at the left and right ends.
Fill the result from the back: put the larger square in the last free slot and move that pointer inward.
explain: The squares are 16, 1, 0, 9 and 100. In ascending order that is `[0,1,9,16,100]`. The largest squares always come from one of the two ends, which is why two pointers work.

title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
summary: In a 1-indexed sorted array, find the two positions whose values add up to target (exactly one answer exists) using O(1) extra space. Return them as [index1, index2].
statement:
`numbers` is sorted in non-decreasing order and uses 1-based positions. Find two different positions whose values add up to `target` and return them as `[index1, index2]` with `index1 < index2`.

Exactly one pair works for every input. Use only constant extra space, so no hash map.
constraints: numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: The array is sorted. If the sum of two values is too small, which value should grow?
Start with one pointer at each end. If the sum is less than target, move the left pointer right; if it is greater, move the right pointer left.
Each step rules out one value for good, so the scan is O(n). Remember to add 1 to both indices in the answer.
explain: 2 + 7 = 9, and 2 and 7 are the first and second numbers. Positions are counted from 1, so the answer is `[1,2]`.

title: Container With Most Water
summary: height[i] is a vertical line at x = i. Pick two lines that, with the x-axis, hold the most water, and return that area.
statement:
`height[i]` is a vertical line standing at `x = i`. Choose two lines; together with the x-axis they form a container. The water it holds is the distance between the lines times the height of the shorter line.

Return the largest amount of water any pair of lines can hold. The container cannot be tilted.
hints: The widest container uses the first and last line. Start there; how could a narrower one ever be bigger?
A narrower container can only win if it is taller. Moving the taller line inward can never help, because the shorter line still limits the height.
Keep two pointers at the ends, record the area, then move the pointer at the shorter line inward. O(n) time.
explain: Use the line of height 8 at index 1 and the line of height 7 at index 8. The water level is the shorter line, 7, and the width is 8 − 1 = 7, so the area is 7 × 7 = 49.

title: 3Sum
summary: Return every unique triplet of values (from different positions) that sums to zero. Triplets may be in any order.
statement:
Return every triplet `[a, b, c]` of values taken from three different positions of `nums` such that `a + b + c == 0`.

Each triplet of values may appear only once in the answer, even if it can be formed from different positions. The triplets, and the values inside them, may be in any order.
hints: Sort the array first. Fixing one value turns the rest into a problem you have seen: two values that add up to a target.
For each index i, run a two-pointer search on the part after i for two values that sum to -nums[i].
Avoid duplicates by skipping an i whose value equals the previous one, and after a match, moving both pointers past repeated values. O(n²) overall.
explain: -1 + -1 + 2 = 0 and -1 + 0 + 1 = 0. The two -1s let you form the first triplet, but each triplet is listed only once, so the answer is `[[-1,-1,2],[-1,0,1]]`.

title: Sort Colors
summary: The array holds only 0, 1 and 2. Sort it in place in one pass without a library sort. The judge prints the array after your call.
statement:
`nums` holds only the values `0`, `1` and `2` (think red, white and blue). Sort it in place so all 0s come first, then the 1s, then the 2s.

Do not use a library sort. Counting the values and rewriting the array works in two passes; the classic solution needs only one pass and constant extra space. The judge prints `nums` after your call.
hints: Keep three regions: 0s at the front, 2s at the back, and an unknown middle you shrink as you go.
Use pointers low, mid and high. A 0 at mid swaps to low (move both forward); a 2 swaps to high (move high back); a 1 just moves mid forward.
After swapping with high, do not advance mid: the value you swapped in has not been looked at yet. Stop when mid passes high.
explain: There are two 0s, two 1s and two 2s, so after sorting in place the array is `[0,0,1,1,2,2]`.

title: Trapping Rain Water
summary: height[i] is the height of a bar of width 1. After rain, how much water is trapped between the bars?
statement:
`height` describes an elevation map: bar `i` has width 1 and height `height[i]`. After it rains, water collects in the dips between taller bars.

Return the total units of water trapped.

The water above bar `i` is the smaller of the tallest bar to its left and the tallest bar to its right, minus `height[i]` (or 0 if that is negative).
hints: Look at one position on its own. How high can the water above it rise?
Water above position i reaches min(tallest bar to its left, tallest bar to its right), minus height[i]. Prefix and suffix maximums give an O(n) solution with O(n) space.
For O(1) space, use two pointers and track leftMax and rightMax. Whichever side has the smaller max is the limiting side, so you can settle that position and move inward.
explain: One unit sits at index 2, between the bars of height 1 and 2. Between the bars of height 2 and 3 four units collect (1 + 2 + 1 at indices 4 to 6). One more sits at index 9. In total 1 + 4 + 1 = 6.

title: Remove Element
summary: Remove every copy of val from nums in place and return k, the number of elements left. The first k slots must hold the kept values, in any order. The judge prints k and the first k elements, sorted.
call: int[] a = BCB.IA($0); int k = s.removeElement(a, BCB.I($1)); int[] f = Arrays.copyOf(a, Math.max(0, Math.min(k, a.length))); Arrays.sort(f); Object r = new Object[] { k, f };
statement:
Remove every occurrence of `val` from `nums` **in place** and return `k`, the number of elements that are not equal to `val`.

After your function returns, the first `k` positions of `nums` must hold exactly those kept values, in any order. What is left beyond position `k` does not matter. The judge prints `k` followed by the first `k` elements sorted, so any order you leave them in is accepted.
hints: You do not need to delete anything. Overwriting is enough, because only the first k slots are checked.
Keep a write index w. Scan every element with a read index.
When the element is not val, copy it to nums[w] and move w forward. At the end, w is k.
explain: Two values in `[3,2,2,3]` are not 3, so k = 2 and the first two slots hold `[2,2]`. The judge prints `[2,[2,2]]`.

title: Reverse String
summary: Reverse the array of characters s in place, using O(1) extra memory. The judge prints s after your call.
statement:
`s` is an array of characters. Reverse it **in place**, so the first character becomes the last and so on.

Use O(1) extra memory: no second array.
hints: The first and last characters swap places, then the second and second-to-last, and so on.
Use two indices, one at each end, and swap the characters they point to.
Move both indices towards the middle and stop when they meet or cross.
explain: Swapping the ends of "hello" and moving inwards gives `["o","l","l","e","h"]`: the h and o swap, the e and second l swap, and the middle l stays put.

title: Valid Palindrome II
summary: Return true if s reads the same forwards and backwards after deleting at most one character.

perf.label: a 99,999-character string
perf.gen: String h = BCB.str(49999, "ab"); String a0 = h.substring(0, h.length() - 1) + "z" + h.charAt(h.length() - 1) + new StringBuilder(h).reverse();

statement:
Return `true` if `s` can become a palindrome (a string that reads the same forwards and backwards) by deleting **at most one** character. Deleting nothing is allowed, so a string that is already a palindrome counts.

For example "abca" also gives `true`: delete the "c" (or the "b") and "aba" is left.
hints: Trying every possible deletion and checking each result is O(n²). Where can the deletion possibly be?
Compare characters from both ends moving inwards. While they match, no deletion is needed.
At the first mismatch, the deleted character must be one of those two. Check whether the rest is a palindrome after skipping the left one, or after skipping the right one.
explain: "aba" already reads the same in both directions, so no deletion is needed and the answer is `true`.

title: Merge Strings Alternately
summary: Build a string by taking letters from word1 and word2 in turn, starting with word1. When one runs out, append the rest of the other.
statement:
Merge `word1` and `word2` by taking letters from them in turn: the first letter of `word1`, then the first letter of `word2`, then the second letter of `word1`, and so on.

If one word is longer, add its remaining letters to the end. Return the merged string.
constraints: `word1` and `word2` have only lowercase English letters
hints: Walk an index i from 0 upwards and look at position i in both words.
Append word1[i] if word1 is long enough, then word2[i] if word2 is long enough.
Stop once i passes the longer word. Use a StringBuilder so building the result stays O(n).
explain: Taking a letter from each word in turn: a, p, b, q, c, r. The merged string is "apbqcr".

title: Merge Sorted Array
summary: nums1 holds m sorted values followed by n spare zeros; nums2 holds n sorted values. Merge nums2 into nums1 in place so nums1 ends up sorted. The judge prints nums1 after your call.
statement:
`nums1` has length `m + n`: its first `m` values are sorted in non-decreasing order and its last `n` slots are zeros you can overwrite. `nums2` holds `n` values, also sorted.

Merge `nums2` into `nums1` **in place** so that `nums1` holds all `m + n` values in sorted order. Don't return anything: the judge prints `nums1` after your call.
hints: Copying nums2 into the spare slots and sorting works in O((m + n) log(m + n)). Can you use the fact that both parts are already sorted?
Merging from the front would overwrite values of nums1 you haven't used yet. The free space is at the back.
Fill nums1 from the end: compare the largest remaining value of each array and write the bigger one at the last free position. Stop when nums2 is used up.
explain: The real values are `[1,2,3]` and `[2,5,6]`. Merged in sorted order they give `[1,2,2,3,5,6]`, which fills all six slots of `nums1`.

title: 4Sum
summary: Return every unique quadruplet of values from nums (four different positions) that adds up to target. Quadruplets, and the values inside them, may be in any order.
statement:
Return every **unique** quadruplet `[nums[a], nums[b], nums[c], nums[d]]` where `a`, `b`, `c` and `d` are four different indices and the four values add up to `target`.

Two quadruplets are the same if they contain the same values. Return them in any order.
hints: This is 3Sum with one more fixed number. Sort the array first so duplicates sit next to each other.
Fix the first two numbers with two nested loops, then find the remaining pair with two pointers moving inwards.
Skip a fixed number when it equals the previous one, and skip repeats after recording a match. Add the four values as long: four values near 10⁹ overflow an int.
explain: Sorted, the array is `[-2,-1,0,0,1,2]`. Three different value sets add up to 0: −2 − 1 + 1 + 2, −2 + 0 + 0 + 2 and −1 + 0 + 0 + 1, so the answer is `[[-2,-1,1,2],[-2,0,0,2],[-1,0,0,1]]`.

title: Rotate Array
summary: Rotate nums to the right by k steps in place: each element moves k places right, wrapping around the end. The judge prints nums after your call.
statement:
Rotate `nums` to the right by `k` steps, **in place**. Each value moves `k` positions to the right, and values pushed off the end wrap around to the front.

`k` can be larger than the array's length. Don't return anything: the judge prints `nums` after your call.
hints: Rotating by k is the same as rotating by k % n, so first reduce k.
With a second array, the value at i moves to (i + k) % n. That is O(n) memory. Can you do it with O(1)?
Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k values, then reverse the rest. Each value lands exactly where it belongs.
explain: Rotating right by one step three times moves 7, 6 and 5 to the front in turn, giving `[5,6,7,1,2,3,4]`.
